techniques.name: The hardest planted pairs are real errors, and the pipeline's filters never check that a plant is one
techniques.claim: On aspire-si's 149 confirmation pairs, the Kev-4B judge fine-tune misses 2-3 pairs per seed order-averaged (2 shared by all three seeds) and 10-12 pairs on single choices (9 shared). The hardest are genuine errors, such as 'must be' changed to 'is usually' known at compile time, and -18 C (0 F) changed to (32 F). aspire-si's pair filters check truncation, no edit, similarity of at least 0.90, length change of at most 5% and self-flag markers; no step verifies that a plant is an error.
techniques.summary: Per-pair rows of the three fine-tuned seeds (rnd experiments/kev-judge-finetune/results/judge-4b-full-s{0,1,2}-confirm.json): single-choice misses are 11/13/12 presentations of 298, 10/12/11 pairs; order-averaged misses 3/2/3. The hardest pairs' edits were read from aspire-si's confirm_set.json edit spans. The filters were read from clean_dataset.py (pair_problems), build_dataset.py and fresh_pairs.py.
techniques.design_implication: A judge's residual misses on planted pairs can be its strongest cases, not its failures: before treating them as judge error, verify each plant is an error. Add a plant-verification step to any planted-error pipeline.
techniques.variance_note: Misses vary by 1-2 pairs between seeds; the shared core is 9 single-choice and 2 order-averaged.
techniques.measured_conditions: Kev-4B judge fine-tune (rnd, 2026-10-07), scored on aspire-si's 149 confirmation pairs.

evals.result: order-averaged 3/2/3 (2 shared); single choice 10/12/11 pairs (9 shared)

techniques.name: Screening natural errors with local judges: gemma4:31b catches almost every flawed answer, muse-glimmer adds sentences
techniques.claim: On 95 llama3.1:8b answers labelled for natural errors, a three-judge local screen (gemma4:31b, mistral-small:24b, granite4.1:30b) flagged every answer that has an error (59 of 59) but only 59 of the 84 error sentences both labelling passes marked (70%). gemma4:31b alone had answer-level recall 0.97 and precision 0.72. muse-glimmer (Meta, 27.9B, Apache-2.0) had answer-level precision and recall of 0.86 and caught 81% of the error sentences; gemma4:31b and muse-glimmer together cover 93%.
techniques.summary: rnd experiments/natural-errors, 2026-10-08. Labels are model-made: claude-opus-5-5 labelled all 95, four blind Sonnet passes labelled them again, and Opus adjudicated the disagreements; the two passes agree at kappa 0.63 (error vs not), Sonnet marking fewer errors, mostly minor ones. The labels are an evaluation yardstick and are not human-verified. muse-glimmer needs plain-text replies: with Ollama's format: json it answered an empty list on all 95. It is the same family as the llama3.1:8b answers, so read it as in-family. Sources: answers by Llama 3.1 8B (Llama 3.1 Community License), questions by Mistral Small 24B (Apache-2.0).
techniques.design_implication: For a natural-error screen, gemma4:31b is the high-recall first pass at the answer level; pair it with a second judge from another family to recover error sentences. Don't force JSON output on muse-glimmer.
techniques.variance_note: 95 answers, one labelling scheme, no human gold.
techniques.measured_conditions: Local Ollama judges on the RTX 5090, 2026-10-08; labels by two Claude passes, adjudicated.

techniques.name: REALMistake: LLM error detectors have low recall on natural errors
techniques.claim: On REALMistake, LLM error detectors including GPT-4 and Claude 3 detected naturally occurring LLM errors at very low recall, far below humans, and majority voting across models and prompts did not help. The Hugging Face dataset card gives cc-by-sa-4.0.
techniques.summary: On REALMistake, LLM error detectors including GPT-4 and Claude 3 detected naturally occurring LLM errors at very low recall, far below humans, and majority voting across models and prompts did not help. The Hugging Face dataset card gives cc-by-sa-4.0.
techniques.design_implication: Don't assume a strong model will catch natural errors; measure recall on natural errors, not only planted ones.

techniques.name: Adding a persona to the system prompt doesn't improve factual accuracy
techniques.claim: Across 162 personas and 4 model families, adding a persona to the system prompt did not improve factual accuracy over a no-persona control, and automatic persona selection was often no better than random.
techniques.summary: Across 162 personas and 4 model families, adding a persona to the system prompt did not improve factual accuracy over a no-persona control, and automatic persona selection was often no better than random.
techniques.design_implication: Design judge or critic roles by their data and training, not by a persona line in the prompt.

techniques.name: Self-Taught Evaluators: synthetic modified-instruction negatives train a strong judge
techniques.claim: Self-Taught Evaluators lifted Llama-3-70B-Instruct from 75.4 to 88.3 on RewardBench (88.7 with majority vote). Negatives from modified instructions scored 83.8, against 80.7 for directly prompted bad responses.
techniques.summary: Self-Taught Evaluators lifted Llama-3-70B-Instruct from 75.4 to 88.3 on RewardBench (88.7 with majority vote). Negatives from modified instructions scored 83.8, against 80.7 for directly prompted bad responses.
techniques.design_implication: When training a judge without human labels, generate negatives by answering a modified instruction rather than asking for a bad answer.

techniques.claim: Merging separately trained pointwise and pairwise judges by weight reached 0.670 Pearson and 79.15% pairwise accuracy, against 0.595 and 75.29% for joint training (averaged columns).
techniques.summary: Merging separately trained pointwise and pairwise judges by weight reached 0.670 Pearson and 79.15% pairwise accuracy, against 0.595 and 75.29% for joint training (averaged columns).
techniques.design_implication: For a judge that must grade both ways, train each format separately and merge weights.

techniques.name: JudgeLM: swap augmentation improves order consistency; more data improves agreement
techniques.claim: Swap augmentation raised JudgeLM-7B's order consistency from 73.45% to 78.89%. Going from 3.5K to 100K training examples raised agreement from 75.87 to 83.71 (7B) and 85.38 to 90.06 (33B).
techniques.summary: Swap augmentation raised JudgeLM-7B's order consistency from 73.45% to 78.89%. Going from 3.5K to 100K training examples raised agreement from 75.87 to 83.71 (7B) and 85.38 to 90.06 (33B).
techniques.design_implication: Train judges on both answer orders; position bias is a training-data problem as much as a model one.

techniques.name: LLMs make correlated errors, more so for larger, more accurate models
techniques.claim: Across 350+ LLMs, on one leaderboard dataset (HELM), two models that both err agree on the same wrong answer about 60% of the time. Shared architectures and providers raise it, and larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even across architectures and providers.
techniques.summary: Across 350+ LLMs, on one leaderboard dataset (HELM), two models that both err agree on the same wrong answer about 60% of the time. Shared architectures and providers raise it, and larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even across architectures and providers.
techniques.design_implication: A jury of strong models is less independent than its size suggests; diversify by family and measure error overlap.

techniques.name: LLM judges favour models similar to themselves; CAPA measures mistake overlap
techniques.claim: LLM-as-a-judge scores favour models similar to the judge, and model mistakes grow more similar with capability. CAPA measures chance-adjusted overlap of mistakes.
techniques.summary: LLM-as-a-judge scores favour models similar to the judge, and model mistakes grow more similar with capability. CAPA measures chance-adjusted overlap of mistakes.
techniques.design_implication: Pick judges from a different family than the models judged, and track mistake overlap with a chance-adjusted measure.

techniques.name: A panel of small judges (PoLL) matches or beats single judges on most QA sets
techniques.claim: PoLL reached Cohen's kappa 0.763 / 0.906 / 0.867 against human judgements on NQ / TriviaQA / HotpotQA. The best single judges were Haiku 0.749 on NQ, CMD-R 0.902 on TriviaQA and Haiku 0.873 on HotpotQA, so PoLL leads on two of three and trails Haiku on HotpotQA.
techniques.summary: PoLL reached Cohen's kappa 0.763 / 0.906 / 0.867 against human judgements on NQ / TriviaQA / HotpotQA. The best single judges were Haiku 0.749 on NQ, CMD-R 0.902 on TriviaQA and Haiku 0.873 on HotpotQA, so PoLL leads on two of three and trails Haiku on HotpotQA.
techniques.design_implication: A small, diverse panel is a strong default judge, but not a guaranteed win on every set.

techniques.name: Just Train Twice: upweighting the first model's errors closes most of the worst-group gap
techniques.claim: JTT closed 75% of the gap in worst-group accuracy between standard training and group DRO, averaged over four tasks, without group labels at training time.
techniques.summary: JTT closed 75% of the gap in worst-group accuracy between standard training and group DRO, averaged over four tasks, without group labels at training time.
techniques.design_implication: When a critic fails on a subgroup of hard pairs, upweight the pairs a first model got wrong before reaching for group labels.

techniques.name: Training on easy data often matches training on hard data
techniques.claim: Models fine-tuned on easy data often performed as well as oracle models fine-tuned on hard data, for open models up to 70B on four QA datasets.
techniques.summary: Models fine-tuned on easy data often performed as well as oracle models fine-tuned on hard data, for open models up to 70B on four QA datasets.
techniques.design_implication: When hard training pairs are scarce or noisy, easy pairs are a reasonable substitute; test before collecting hard data at cost.
